speechtext:
Right Hon. J, G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, arising out of an answer I gave to the Leader of the Opposition as recorded on page 358 of Hansard for January 27, 1959, when he referred to the omission of the mayor of Ottawa and the mayor of Hull from the national capital commission. On that occasion I said, speaking from memory, as follows:
In the Federal District Commission Act provision was specifically made that the mayor of Ottawa and the mayor of Hull should be members of the commission.
I now find that the statement I made was inadvertently incorrect. Under the act as it originally was, section 3, subsection 3, provision was made as follows:
One member shall be appointed by the corporation of the city of Ottawa to hold office during pleasure-
Under subsection 4 of the same section we find this:
One member shall be appointed by the corporation of the city of Hull to hold office during pleasure-
In view of the fact the mayors of the two cities had been members of the federal district commission, I associated that section with the fact they were members and thought it made provision for the mandatory appointment of the mayors, while in point of fact the appointment was made by the council of each of these cities. I thought I ought to point out my inadvertence of yesterday.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 22, 1959 the Leader of the Opposition asked the following question:
I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether any representations have been made to the United States government concerning the revival of the Hyde park agreement and particularly the combined defence production board which operated so successfully under that agreement during the war.
My answer is that there have been no representations made to the United States government concerning the revival of the Hyde park declaration of April 20, 1941, and the reason for the lack of representations is that representations were not required. The Leader of the Opposition will recall full
[Mr. Nowlan.l

well, I am sure, that there was no terminal date to the declaration, the text of which, I set forth for the record, may be found in the Canada treaty series, 1941, No. 14.
Provision was made, however, for the continuance of the principles of the Hyde park declaration into the post-war period in an exchange of notes with the United States government in May, 1945. The text of this exchange is contained in the same series, 1948, No. 1. The purposes of the exchange were explained to the house on February 13, 1948 by Mr. St. Laurent, who was then secretary of state for external affairs.
Again in October, 1950 provision was made for the further extension of the principles of the Hyde park declaration in the statement of principles for economic co-operation. The exchange of relevant correspondence appears in Canada treaty series, 1950, No. 15.
Current discussions between representatives of the two governments on the question of sharing of defence production tasks have of course been carried out against the background and on the basis of these and related intergovernmental agreements.
The board to which I presume the Leader of the Opposition made reference must be the Canadian-United States joint war production committee which was established for specific purposes in November 1941 and which was dissolved on December 31, 1945. Representations have not been made to the United States government concerning the revival of this particular board. However, new machinery of consultation with the United States government on the question of defence production sharing has been established and is working to the satisfaction of both governments.
I understand that the Minister of Defence Production plans to make, in the near future, a comprehensive statement on the question of the sharing of defence production tasks in North America, which will provide further details on this subject which may be of interest to the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. Jorgenson for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
last evening just before ten o'clock I made reference to the commonwealth trade and economic conference held in Montreal last September. To provide continuity with my remarks today and also because of the importance of the conference itself I wish to repeat in summary some of the observations I made last evening.
On the basis of fact the Montreal conference was unique, and I use that term "unique" in the sense of the definition in Murray's English dictionary where the word is defined as meaning not only alone of its kind, but more particularly in this case as meaning "standing alone in comparison with others". This conference was unique in a number of ways, of which I shall cite three.
First of all the representation from the commonwealth included all the older members plus many new ones from Asia and Africa with representation to, and therefore through, the United Kingdom; of Nigeria, the West Indies, Kenya, Tanganyika, Uganda, Sierra Leone and Hong Kong, to such an extent that the new members outnumbered the old.
It was also unique in that the agenda was not limited. It included the widest possible range of subjects in keeping with an expanding commonwealth in a world with a growing list of new states. Furthermore it was unique

The Address-Mr. Vivian in regard to the wide area of general agreement which was reached in these difficult times.
As to the results of this conference, I believe they are also unique. This opinion is based on occurrences immediately after the conference, last autumn, at the general assembly of the United Nations, which if they are true indicators, as I believe they are, foretell a new spirit and a new desire to deal with the problems of international trade in a way more beneficial than in the past to the world community as a whole. Again I make specific reference to the fact that the United States delegation to the United Nations general assembly committee on economic and financial matters accepted and supported the language of a resolution on international commodity trade which was subsequently adopted, the wording of which was taken directly from the commonwealth report. This is the farthest the United States has ever been prepared to go in such matters. I maintain that the results of the Montreal conference are already unique, but of course continuity of this kind must be maintained.
I must point out that actions taken at the United Nations general assembly have their limitations, and no one in this house knows about those limitations better than the present Leader of the Opposition. The 82 member states that comprise the general assembly of the United Nations cannot take such action as will bind all members of sovereign states to implement the majority opinion. They can only make recommendations. Action of this sort in the United Nations can only be preliminary to the action of each sovereign state; but it can create, and in this case I trust it has created by overwhelming agreement a favourable climate in which similar action will be taken by those sovereign states in particular agreements. This is what is meant by the successful cultivation of a garden.
I wish to point out other words in the gracious speech from the throne which show the present government's intention regarding Canada's position in world affairs, in respect of economic assistance to underdeveloped countries and expansion of the resources of the international bank and the international monetary fund. Economic assistance to less developed countries may be provided in a variety of ways. Time will not permit me to deal extensively with this subject, and it would be better dealt with on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. I should like, however, to indicate the nature and purpose of Canada's participation.
Our participation in economic assistance has been mainly through the Colombo plan and the United Nations. The Colombo plan, as you will recall, is a matter of country to


country assistance, and in this instance much of the money provided by the donor country may be spent in that donor country in terms of material supplies or for the salaries of technical assistants, whereas through the United Nations our aid and the aid of other countries is given on a multilateral basis. Funds are donated to projects in which all the donor countries share without any direct country to country relationship.
The question might be asked if the financial assistance provided through the United Nations and Colombo plan could be classed as a give-away program. In the opinion of many experienced persons, an opinion in which I wish to join, the answer is emphatically no, because the well-being of each of the countries of the world, now so interrelated with the well-being of all, is a vital matter upon which satisfactory progress must be made because it is really necessary for the peace of our time.
There are now such vast areas of the world emerging into nationhood, many with strong anti-colonial feelings, that their progress concerns all of us. The rate of growth from dependent territory to sovereign state is very rapid. This, of course, is accompanied by local pressures from domestic, economic and social demands. In many areas the situation is one which can best be described in the words of the Prime Minister of India, Mr. Nehru, as the revolution of rising expectation. This is an exhilarating and possibly dangerous time, Mr. Speaker.
Canada is looked to as a friendly country, without any aspirations to dominate the development of others, so our reputation is exceedingly high. In part this may be due to our relative generosity in helping others less fortunate than ourselves, but it is also due in large part to the regard for Canada in our own evolutionary progress from colony to statehood. Under these circumstances Canada's help is needed by the less developed countries, these new emerging states. It is not only needed, Mr. Speaker, but it must be provided to the best of our ability. This is not a matter merely of economic assistance; it is also a question, I think of equal importance, of our understanding of the problems of the less developed countries. In this matter Canada is in a position to help.
I might point out here, sir, that while we might be willing to give help it is something which must be requested. I refer again to the feelings of the people of many of these territories now emerging into statehood. They wish to do those things that they consider to be necessary for their own wellbeing and to increase their own standard of living by themselves, in so far as possible.

Our watch word in this connection should be, not only should we do unto others as we would have them do unto us, but we should do unto others as they would wish us to do for them. The objective of all this is to stand by and be ready to help so the less developed countries may achieve the fullest possible measure of their potential as responsible states in the world.
I welcome again the words in the gracious speech that apply to the underdeveloped countries of Asia and Africa, and particularly at this time Africa where new states will soon face the heavy responsibilities that come with independence. Our aid, in all its forms, is dependent upon our own stability and our own continued economic progress. Canada, like the rest of the world, has had a bit of tough going recently. In this connection, however, we are more fortunate than many others. We are fortunate in a variety of ways, but at this particular time we are exceedingly fortunate in having a government in power that recognizes Canada's problems, that acts on those problems with expert advice, and is prepared to look beyond our own now improving economic situation, to the action we will be called upon to take in world affairs.
It is therefore my privilege, Mr. Speaker, to support wholeheartedly the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do that not out of form or habit. I really enjoyed their remarks, though it was necessary for me to read the translation of one speech. I feel that they have both done themselves credit and have brought distinction to their respective constituencies.
Before I go on to make some remarks concerning the speech from the throne I should like to make a few remarks concerning my own riding. First of all, on behalf of my people I must say that we are extremely pleased that in June Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip will visit my home city. Since in the cross-country tour the Queen, of course, will not have an opportunity to visit every place in any one constituency, and there will be an opportunity for her to see only a small part of the constituency, I would hope that the time available to Her Majesty would allow her to see the beautiful Codroy valley in my constituency, to be able to ride up the Humber river or to view, I am sure with gratification, the scenery that can be observed at Bonne Bay on the west coast
The Address-Mr. Batten of Newfoundland. Time, of course, is not such that she will be able to do all this; but whatever time she will be able to spend on the west coast of Newfoundland will be extremely pleasing to my people, and I know they will afford her that hospitality which is not only characteristic of Newfoundlanders but also that which befits the visit of our Queen.
My home city is situated on Bay of Islands, 30 miles inland. It is a new city with a population of 25,000. Here is situated the largest integrated newsprint mill in the world, with the possible exception of Powell river in British Columbia. The city of Corner Brook is a large distribution centre, with the result that during all times in the year a great deal of tonnage is coming into the harbour and a great deal of tonnage is going out. Last year I had the opportunity of placing on record the tonnages for a number of years past. I am not going to do that now. However, I contend that the port of Corner Brook is of some considerable importance.
In the winter time, of course, we experience the difficulty of having our port closed for two or three months by ice. Again, as I have done on previous occasions, I make an appeal to the Minister of Transport that in making his plans for icebreaking in the lower St. Lawrence and in the gulf, he include the port of Corner Brook. Representations have been made to the minister by the labour unions in the area, the chamber of commerce and other interested bodies. The ideal situation would be if an icebreaker could be placed there all winter. If it is not possible at the moment for that to be done, I think the minister should take into consideration the need for icebreaking facilities in the port and that he should distribute, as far as it is possible to do so, the icebreakers so that some service can be given to this particular area.
There is another point I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker, and bring to the attention of the Postmaster General. He is well aware of the fact that along the coast of Newfoundland are numerous small post offices. These people are obliged to provide their own accommodation. They are obliged to provide their heat and the janitor service for the building which is rented. In nearly every case in these small post offices the remuneration is not sufficient to make it worth while for anybody to discharge these services to the community. As I go around my riding I find many of these postmasters and postmistresses who are complaining about the amount of money they receive for services rendered.
I should like to recommend to my hon. friend that when he is reviewing the position with regard to these small post offices, some

The Address-Mr. Batten upward revision be made in the remuneration which these people are receiving, if that action is at all possible. I fear that if this is not done we are at some time going to arrive at the point where these people are going to feel that the service they are rendering is no longer being compensated for, and they will not be willing to continue to render that service which is extremely important to these small places along the coast of Newfoundland.
On an earlier occasion I made some reference to the telegraph facilities along the west coast of Newfoundland. I now bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Transport again. Some years ago-30 years ago, to be exact-there was a satisfactory telegraph service down the north coast or the northwest coast of Newfoundland. Over the years part of this service, or at least part of the facilities for the service, has been taken away and has not been replaced. I recognize the fact that, as far as Canadian National Telegraphs are concerned, their interest is in receiving some revenue for the outlay they make. I agree that this is probably an area in which they will not receive any great revenue for the expenditure they will be obliged to make. But somewhere between revenue that is worth while and no revenue at all there surely must come into the picture the question of service.
These people at the present time are receiving a telegraph service which is surely not satisfactory in this day and age. Last year I recommended to the Minister of Transport that if Canadian National Telegraphs were not able to look after this area on a business basis, it might be taken over by the Department of Transport and operated as a service. But whatever the solution to the problem may be, Mr. Speaker, I believe that some serious consideration needs to be given to this problem so the people who live in these outlying areas will at least have the benefit of a first class telegraph service.
On that coast there are some hospitals. They are widely spaced. In emergencies it is necessary to contact the doctor at the hospital or a nurse along the coast. Unless the facilities are provided these people feel that they are not receiving the health service which can be provided for them. I would therefore again recommend to the minister that some serious consideration be given to this urgent problem.
I must apologize to the house for raising one more point again, but I fear that I shall be obliged to do so. Last year during the discussion of the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I referred to radio station CBY at Corner Brook. This is the only C.B.C. radio station on the west coast of Newfoundland. Many persons depend upon

this station for news and other bits of information which are important to a people who live along the coast, long distances from any large centre.
That radio station is operating on a frequency of 790 kilocycles. Some time ago another station in Newcastle, New Brunswick, was opened and operated on the same frequency. These two stations interfere with one another to such an extent that to the north of Corner Brook where the station is situated and to the south of Corner Brook people are not able to receive the C.B.C. station at Corner Brook. What the remedy is I do not know. The remedy may be a change in the frequency; it may be a change in the ground pattern, or a change in the power. That matter is, of course, one to be dealt with by a radio engineer.
However, I would suggest that this is a serious problem to the people concerned. Again I appeal to the Minister of National Revenue, who speaks for the C.B.C. in this house, to make some effort to have this situation remedied so these people will be able to enjoy the benefits of radio at a time when a large percentage of the people in this country are enjoying the benefits of television.
We have no C.B.C. television in Newfoundland as such. There is a private station in St. John's, CJON, which I believe is well run and gives excellent television coverage. On the west coast of Newfoundland at the United States air force base at Stephenville there is a television station which is run jointly by the C.B.C. and the United States government but there is no C.B.C. television in Newfoundland as such. They are now building a television station at Corner Brook, a city with a population of 25,000 and with a population in the area which could be covered of nearly 50,000. It has come to my attention that the station which is being built in Corner Brook will not be sufficiently powerful to cover the nearby town of Deer Lake with 7,000 people, only 30 miles away. I would hope that this statement is not true. I appeal to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) to see that the power of the station being built at Corner Brook is sufficiently great to be able to give television coverage to the people within the city, to the people within the Bay of Islands and to the people who live in the town of Deer Lake.
I know that the people north of there in Bonne Bay will not be able to receive the station. Maybe at some time they will be able to receive the services of a new station built to provide service in that particular area.

I listened with care to and I have since read, the speech from the throne. I suppose most speeches from the throne are important for what they mention at some length. They are important, too, for the things they just barely mention and they are sometimes important for the things which are omitted. This particular speech from the throne may give us some idea of what the government's policy is for the present session but it does, in my opinion, give very scant attention to some of the problems which face us as a people at this time.
During the debate which we have had here on the speech from the throne I have been a little interested in the attitude of the government toward criticism which has been directed at them. They have taken the attitude that it is the responsibility of the opposition to criticize and to offer alternative suggestions. That, of course, is quite true, but both of these things imply that in the first place there must be something to criticize, and in the second place there must be a policy to which an alternative can be offered. It does seem to me that in many of the operations of the government there are criticisms which can be made. When members of the government say, "What did you do?'' I feel that that interjection has long been worn out. The government has now been in power long enough to make its own policy. It is going to have to make its own decisions and it is going to have to stand or fall on those decisions. That is the price of power, Mr. Speaker.
I do not think the government and the government members are able to go on forgetting the fact that they must now be responsible for their own policies and they must be able to support them. The time is not too far away when we are going to be out of the post-election years and into the pre-election years when the policy of the government is going to have to be defended. I feel that no party will ever gain as much support from criticizing the opposition now as it did in the last election. Therefore, whatever policies are presented by the government now must be defended within the short space of two, three or four years. Therefore I do not quite understand the attitude which the government takes when it talks about the criticism which has been hurled at them. However, maybe the government feels that it can defend its own policies better by answering those criticisms and that, of course, is their decision.
I refer, Mr. Speaker, to the very serious problem of unemployment. Maybe there is no part of Canada where unemployment is such a serious problem as it is in the province from which I come. The year 1958 was not
The Address-Mr. Batten a good one in Newfoundland. The codfish in the sea did not pay us the benefit of very many visits. Our fishermen have not been able to catch the amount of fish that would give them a normal income for the year. The fall fisheries, particularly the herring fishery in Port au Port bay, have been a complete failure. We have not had nearly as much work in the paper industry as we have had in other years. There have been reductions in the actual operation of the mill itself as well as in the lumbering industry, and at the moment we are faced with some very serious labour problems. All in all it has been a very bad year for Newfoundland.
I concur wholeheartedly in the action taken by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) when last fall he wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and asked that something be done in this regard. It is all very well to talk about the number of people who are unemployed, the number of people who are looking for jobs and the number of people who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits, but I think that maybe the one statistic that will point up the seriousness of this problem in Newfoundland is the fact that today there are nearly 42,000 people in a population of 420,000, 10 per cent, receiving relief from the provincial government, apart altogether from those who have no jobs and are receiving unemployment insurance. Forty-two thousand out of a population of 420,000, 10 per cent, are now on provincial government relief, and I think that one figure alone is sufficient to point up the seriousness of this situation in the province from which I come.
It is indeed true that in some places the winter works program has given some employment to many people. I still feel that the winter works program which will provide work for 15,000, 20,000 or 25,000 people is still not sufficient to be able to reduce substantially the large number of people who are out of work in this country. There are places in Newfoundland, for instance, where a winter works program can be instituted and where a good deal of winter work can be carried on. There are other places where this cannot be done, and I think that in places where such a program cannot be carried out the solution of the whole problem is to make sure that whatever federal works -and I include provincial works as well- whatever government works are going to be carried on in the following year should be prepared for in such a way that as soon as the spring comes these jobs can get under way and be started in March, April or May rather than in June, July or August.
I repeat that in the places which are not likely to be serviced by any large amount

The Address-Mr. Batten of winter work the thing to do is to make sure that whatever work is to be done in the spring will be started early so that those people who need employment will be able to get it at the earliest possible time.
There is, of course, the twin problem of inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), in his reply to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), said, "Well, we have always had inflation", and that, of course, is quite true. But he might have gone on to say that the world has had it for the last 4,000 years. But during that time there are very few if any examples of countries which have allowed inflation to run uncontrolled, which have been able to come out of this problem without financial chaos. I think we have always had inflation. We have it now and I think we will have it in the future. I do not blame the government for inflation, but surely we are going to have to blame the government if they should allow it to run uncontrolled. It will do this nation of Canada a great deal of harm if the proper controls are not instituted at the appropriate time and early enough to be able to have their effect during the coming year.
In other countries, or in some other countries at least, where they are not bound by the terms of a constitution as we are, and are not subject to the secrecy of a budget, they are able to introduce measures to control inflation at a very early date. We are not in that fortunate position, and I suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that whatever measures he has in mind for the control of inflation should be stated clearly in the budget, and that the budget should be presented at the earliest possible date.
One thing I did notice in the speech from the throne which is very important to the people of Newfoundland was the item concerning freight rates. We live at the end of the line, and living at the end of the line we have the long haul. On the long haul the people at the end must pay the highest freight rates. During the last ten years we have seen almost as many increases in freight rates and these increases have placed on the people of Newfoundland a great burden. We live in a province where nearly everything we produce has to be shipped out of the province and where nearly everything we use has to be brought in, with the result that freight rates play a very important part in our lives. We do not have the advantage, as some other provinces do, of a network of roads where much trucking is carried on. Our transportation of goods and commodities is carried on mostly either by C.N.R. boats or by C.N.R. trains, and when there is an increase in freight 
rates it places an added burden on people who live in a province such as Newfoundland or in provinces in the west of Canada. I was pleased to note that some consideration was being given to this problem. I do not know what conclusion the Prime Minister will reach, but I hope it will be such as to alleviate some of the ills which have their source in the continuing increase in the cost of handling and shipping freight.
I referred earlier to the fisheries of Newfoundland. Of course, the failure of the fisheries is not by any means the fault of the government. I must be fair and admit that the fact that the codfish did not come to Newfoundland is not the government's fault. But I do wish to say that if the fishery in Newfoundland is to be prosecuted profitably in the years that lie ahead the government must provide for the fishermen the things they are not able to provide for themselves. The fishermen are not able to provide for themselves the many marine works that are needed along the coast.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) has made some progress in regard to bait depots. There are only a very few of these depots in existence at the present time. How they will work out we have yet to ascertain, but I want to tell the minister now that we are going to need many more of these installations along the coast if they are to give to the fishermen the service which will allow them to prosecute their occupation profitably. I believe that the fisheries of Newfoundland can be of continuing importance to Newfoundland and to Canada, but this is only true provided that those things needed for the successful prosecution of the industry are provided for these men who cannot provide them for themselves.
I was interested, too, in the reference in the speech from the throne to the trans-Canada highway. I do not at this time intend to place on record again comparative figures as to the cost of building a trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland and elsewhere. I do not think that to compare cost per mile of the trans-Canada highway is the proper way to make a cost comparison when one is dealing with people and the taxes which they pay. I think the proper way to compare the cost is to compute it on the basis of numbers of people. Last year I placed on record the number of miles of the trans-Canada highway which would have to be built by a group of 10,000 people both in Newfoundland and in every province across this country; and the number of miles of the trans-Canada highway to be built by a group of 10,000 people in Newfoundland is far greater than in any other province in Canada. If there is any

added assistance which can be given toward the building of the trans-Canada highway- and I hope there will be-I hope it will be provided, and provided soon, so that we can get along with this job and build the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland not only to provide work but also to give us a better transportation system.
We live in a province which has an outdated railway. It is one of those narrow gauge railways which over the years has given fine service. It gave yeoman service during the second world war. However, I feel it is outdated in many ways, not only because it is a narrow gauge. Sometime, maybe the C.N.R. or the government will consider the building of a railway of regular gauge in Newfoundland so that we way receive the same service as that which people on the mainland enjoy. In any case, building the trans-Canada highway will assist our transportation facilities which at the present time are not too good. Whatever assistance can be given in this respect I hope can be given early. It has always been my belief, and I have said so in this house before, that when the Canadian government decided it was going to enter into an agreement with the provinces to build a trans-Canada highway across Canada it should have built the whole road and been done with it. I still think that should have been done. However, any increased allocation which can be granted toward the building of this road will be very welcome in the province from which I come.
I could not leave this subject without taking the opportunity to make some reference to federal-provincial relations. We remember that before the election in 1957 the Prime Minister went across this country saying that if he were elected he would call a federal-provincial conference immediately. Well, he was elected. He did not call a conference immediately, but he did call one late in November. I attended that conference- the part of it which was public-and I went away with the feeling that what was done could easily have been done by mail; the same result could have been accomplished if the premiers had just made their reports and sent them in so the Prime Minister would know what they were thinking. However, at that conference the Prime Minister said he was not going to adopt any take it or leave it attitude. The premiers came, they made their statements and they went home with the promise that they would meet again early in January. That conference was never called, and the Prime Minister was remarkably reticent on this subject from then on. Then we come, of course, to the famous telegrams sent by the Minister of Finance in
The Address-Mr. Batten December of 1957 telling the provinces what they were going to get. Here again was the adoption of a take it or leave it attitude. In the speech from the throne we now hear that this particular method is to be adopted for another year, and once again we are faced with a take it or leave it attitude. In the meantime the problem of arriving at agreement between the federal government and the provinces remains unsolved and is no further toward a solution than it was when the Prime Minister talked about it in the pre-election days of 1957.
While talking about federal-provincial relations I cannot resist making some reference to the McNair commission. Hon. members will be aware that the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada include a provision, term 29, which states that after a period of eight years there would be some revision of the finances of the province. This situation arose because when the terms of union were drawn up it was impossible to forecast what the financial effect of the union would be upon the province of Newfoundland. With the knowledge we have after the event I do not suppose anyone will deny that when we came into power in June of 1957 unemployment was on the increase. By August this was obvious and we took steps to counteract it. I am not going to get involved in a long argument about inheritance or inheriting. I will just make this point from which I do not think my friend, with all his footwork, can get away. Either we inherited something or we changed the economic situation of this country between June and August. Is anyone going to argue that we did that? Is anyone going to argue that what was done in August to meet unemployment was occasioned by what we had done between June and August? I do not think any sensible man will. In August counter-measures were taken. The sum of $150 million was set apart for housing, and I need not do more than recall what has happened since. The amount has steadily risen and is now $750 million. I also notice in the afternoon paper an announcement that the amount is going to be raised.
Furthermore, the employment that has come from that is far greater and came about far more quickly than could have happened in any other way. On December 1 the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) said that it would provide 250,000 jobs this winter, and that is only what are called on-site jobs. There is in addition all the indirect work provided to workers on materials, and it is estimated that the off-site employment provided is practically as great as on-site. Then there is, in addition, the ordinary government expenditures of the various departments which account for some 150,000 more jobs. This winter, in addition, we have made an offer to the municipalities, coupled with the provinces to help provide employment, under which I think nearly 1,100 projects have been accepted and something like 19,000 men have been put to work, if my memory serves me correctly.

I am sorry the Leader of the Opposition spoke of the commonwealth conference at Montreal in a rather contemptuous fashion. I had the good fortune to be there, and while we should not exaggerate, should not pretend that it did more than make a beginning toward solving problems. No one who was there could accept the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition, who seemed to think it was a matter of a few boxes of salmon and some yards of calico. It was not that at all. Practical steps were taken, but what was really the important thing and what impressed everyone who was there was the spirit.
I hope I am not an unduly emotional man but I confess to you I was impressed by seeing men of different colours, races and religions meeting together as friends and partners. It was impressive to me, the last morning we were there, to hear one of the African delegates, who was just as different from us in every way as it was possible to be, use the phrase, "We of the commonwealth".
What was this spirit? What did it amount to, where did it come from and to what point could it lead us? The answer to these questions depends a great deal upon ourselves. Indo-China, and what is happening there, may be a turning point in our history. What is happening in Geneva may bring the commonwealth closer to the United States than ever before. I was impressed first of all by the fact it was being done and in the second place, I was impressed by their attitude and their desire to be associated with the rest of us and to play a part with the rest of us. Incidentally I may say that I am told that they have conducted themselves extremely well in the United Nations. I want to read further from the Prime Minister's words as follows:
