What an accurate forecast that was of what has been happening and is still happening. In the light of this, in the light of what he had been saying for years, he did not lose a day. When he became Prime Minister he went straight to London and there, as we all know, he pressed for and succeeded in having a commonwealth conference held.
My time is short, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to say something of this commonwealth. When I was in Malaya the thought struck me, as it never had before, of the world-wide extent of the commonwealth; with one country in America; one in Europe; four, if I remember right, in Asia; two in the south seas; and three in Africa; it spans the world. The hon. member for Essex East has been there and he will endorse this. It is an example of a world order on a small scale. We are in North America but we are also in the commonwealth. Australia is in the south Seas but it is also in the commonwealth. Malaya is in Asia but it is also in the commonwealth. The Prime Minister was quick to realize this truth. Actually, it is almost a miracle that it exists as it does. Would anyone have visualized 10 or 15 years ago that if India were given its freedom, and particularly if it became a republic, it would still stay in the commonwealth? I will venture to say that anyone to whom that proposition was made would have thought it to be silly. However, it exists because of understanding and common purpose and a common belief in the dignity and the importance of the individual or, in other words, freedom. I saw this in Malaya.
All this is true and important, but it is not the whole truth. Men who are starving will in the end prefer food to freedom. That is the reason why we must see that they are not left with this dreadful choice. In other words, we must see that they can be developed to the point where they can feed their populations. The solution, of course, is to help develop the underdeveloped countries. This thought was in everyone's mind at Montreal when the conference took place. It seems to me it is a pity that we should be splitting hairs as to whether the conference led up to or foreshadowed the currency arrangements which were made afterwards. I think we have some important things to talk about other than that. The Prime Minister realized it. Here is what he told the people at Sydney when he went around the world to follow up the conference. He
442	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell realized it was just the beginning. He realized more had to be done. He said to the people in Sydney:
I came for the purpose of seeing members of this commonwealth and, in particular, those who, as you said a moment ago, are located in Asia where I believe, as I have said on other occasions, the success or failure of the endeavour among our nations to achieve not only a common heritage but also, in achieving that, to ensure a high degree of economic prosperity each for the other will depend upon whether or not this commonwealth can live, expand and develop as I expect and anticipate it will.
I believe these are matters of vast importance for us to think about. We must not regard it as a kind of super community drive. We must regard it as a task which faces us not merely because other people are badly off, but in our own interests because it is essential for us to live in an expanding world, as was said at the conference. This world must expand to the point where the underdeveloped countries can develop and trade and in that way to the point where we can all prosper.
I think it is absolutely essential that we should all get an entirely new conception of the duties and responsibilities that lie on us before it is too late; and when I say "too late", I mean "too late". I sometimes wonder whether we in North America are not like children playing in the sand. Of course, we seem to be far off from danger but we now know that nobody is far off. I sometimes wonder whether we are taking ourselves seriously enough when we enjoy all the things that we have and seem to have so little time for thinking of the responsibilities which face us. Whether right or wrong, whether we were doing it well or ill, when we were at Montreal we were trying to face these things. I regret more than I can say that all the opposition could do was to try to play it down. I want to read to you from what the Prime Minister said at Royal Albert hall on November 4. He puts the matter clearly and inescapably. Here are some of his words:
I want to assure you in simple language that our desire is to contribute to the strength and the spirit of the commonwealth and to the common welfare of its peoples. When you see the peoples in Asia you realize that if all we bring before them is the promise of parliamentary government, stomachs are not filled with that.
Later he said this:
I think it is idle for men to speak of peace, of freedom and parliamentary democracy, unless the association can meet the basic needs, the economic needs of the various peoples comprising this family of nations.
Mr. Speaker, my time is up. I hope that my words have perhaps carried some conviction. I hope that we shall recognize the 

responsibilities that we face and that we shall not wake up one day and say to ourselves, "Why did we not think about that before? Nobody ever told us". The Prime Minister has told us. I hope we will register his words, take them seriously and act accordingly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very easy for me to offer congratulations to the hon. gentleman who moved the address (Mr. Jorgenson). He was on the NATO parliamentary junket with me, and if it is permissible for one member to say it about another, I thought he was well above the average in both ability and insight. I did not have the opportunity of hearing the speech made by the seconder (Mr. Fortin). I read it. I noticed it received tremendous commendation in the press and I personally, after reading it, felt that it was in the long tradition. It seems that ever since Lord Durham let the black cat out of the bag in 1837, one of the things English and French Canadians like to do when they get together is to be very sweet to each other and talk in terms of national unity and how well things are going. I have nothing against that at all but I sometimes feel there is a sweeping change taking place in French Canada and I, for one, as someone who lives a long distance away from it, would wish that we could have recapitulated in this house some of the views of this new Quebec that would remind us more of what Professor Lower has put down, and I think correctly, namely the fact that because we have French and English in Canada it forms our primary antithesis. I certainly say this, we should hear an explanation from English and French speaking members from Quebec of their views in the controversy centring around the Tremblay report.
In this matter of French Canada being on the move, I have heard a rather interesting little remark from a French-Canadian friend of mine about the C.B.C. strike in Montreal; that this was the most unusual thing that ever happened; for the first time the French-Canadian intellectuals seemed to be working with the labour movement in Quebec. I said, "This certainly would be unusual because from my reading of the Quebec press the French-Canadian intellectuals seem to spend most of their time worrying about invasions upon the purity of the French-Canadian language." This chap said, "Wait, my friend. In six months time they will be worrying about the purity of the labour movement", which, if it should happen, would be most interesting.
In the remarks I have just made I would not like to leave the suggestion that the fact of national unity is something that we need

to dismiss. I think that the last prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, combined in his person a tremendous charm reflecting both branches of Canada. He did a great deal just in his restatement of platitudes in moving us toward national unity, but I still think it is not going to be resolved without far more discussion and the cross current of debate. I do not mean the kind of debate that seems to develop so often in this chamber by French-Canadian members on a partisan basis which seems to be a mere matter of black and white and white and black.
One cannot help but welcome the translation device which is available to us all. The only thing I would like to remark in connection with the arrangements in the chamber is that there has been a threat to cut down on the reading of speeches. I sometimes think that we will be just beating ourselves against a feather pillow in attacking the problem. One of the things that might be suggested here is that at the party caucuses, instead of worrying about reading of speeches, we could give some lessons in reading.
One of the things that bothers me in the reply that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) gave to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in this particular debate is his delicate sensitivity with regard to criticism of his trip beyond the seas. I have been puzzled as to why he is so peculiarly sensitive in this regard. I heard him make the remark that a statesman was a dead politician. In other words, he recognizes that he is a politician. I think he is also aware that world trips give glamour and prestige which may be reflected in that crass but very important place, the polling booth. Surely he cannot blame other politicians for trying to set a balance against that glamour and prestige. I certainly found that it was a most interesting trip. I know that some of the Scottish people in my constituency were delighted to discover that the Prime Minister went looking for his Scottish ancestors. Many did not realize that he had Scottish ancestors. I only hope that everything went well for him in that search. I know a friend of mine a few years ago went and looked up the kirk records in Scotland to trace his ancestors on his father's side. He discovered that his great great grandfather, who was born in the middle of the 18th century, was illegitimate and had been just a charge upon the parish. This was quite embarrassing and he sloughed off his interest in geneology.
One of the other things about the Prime Minister's trip that I know interested many people in my constituency was the dispatch out of Rome that a photographer was absent,
The Address-Mr. Fisher unfortunately, when the Prime Minister was having his interview with the Pope, and I quite frankly say that photograph would have been worth a great deal to the Prime Minister in electoral terms.
The part about the world tour that I appreciated most was the homely and amusing story that came out of Lahore, India. To a Kipling reader the snarling of tigers and the trumpeting of elephants and the whole exotic orient portrayed in those books creates a magic spell. Thus to a Kiplingite the remark of one prominent member of the Canadian delegation was wonderful. After the party had watched a display of the whirling dervishes he said that they reminded him very much of the shriners in Canada at a convention.
Later on when the Prime Minister came arrowing home across the very romantic south Pacific, it just happened to coincide with a very severe cold wave in Port Arthur. The batteries in our cars were frozen and the radiators were frozen and the thermometer stood at 30 degrees below zero. The unemployment percentages happened to be rising above 20 per cent of the labour force and, as a consequence, certain feelings welled up naturally at the thought of this exotic trip in contrast with what one poor member of parliament was suffering in his constituency.
In making these remarks one would like to remind the Prime Minister that we do not want that Gallup poll to go right up to the top. If it goes much higher I am sure he will request that we all get out of here. I would ask him and the Conservatives to be a little less sensitive with regard to this world trip.
One of the things that I must credit the Leader of the Opposition for is the exceptionally good speech he made this year compared with what was referred to that in January of last year-a relative failure. Certainly, after the speech the Prime Minister did not come rushing into the abattoir in the way that he was described as doing last time. I thought there was rather an excellent selection of material in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and that congratulations should go to Professors Lamontagne and McEachen. Carlyle once said that economics is the dismal science, and these gentlemen are professors of economics. This may be the explanation for the certain gloomy quality in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, which the ranks of the government have bleated about.
One of the things I noticed the Leader of the Opposition referred to, and it has been referred to by other hon. members here, is the performance and denunciations of the

The Address-Mr. Fisher hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne). I was delighted, Mr. Speaker, to discover that the views of the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska had even reached France, not Paris, which is the heart of the nation, but the relatively provincial city of Lyon, France. Here is a newspaper called L'Annonceur Francais for December 31, 1958, and who is on the front page in connection with an analysis of the political situation in Canada, none other than the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska. It is in French. My translating abilities are not exceptional, but I did translate this, and it fits in nicely with the way the hon. member's remarks have been used in the past. The member of parliament for Restigouche-Madawaska said:
We appreciate that you have helped us to accomplish our work.
He was speaking to a very large association in New Brunswick last August. I gather the people belonged to L'Union des electeurs. I continue with the translation:
We always find money by the million and by the billion when it is for war. Why can't we find money to double the family allowances? The politicians have their eyes closed to misery, we should open them wide and quickly as we do in the case of war.
It is inexcusable that in a country as rich as Canada that there are still people reduced to living in poverty, yes, even in black misery. If this is not the fault of the government then whose fault is it?
This part is interesting, and it suggests a new tack in the career of the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska:
The monetary principles that we know are insane. The only answer is to proclaim this with all your tenacity to show the absurdity and the barbarism of our actual finance system.
That was the end of the reported remarks of the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska. There was a quotation from the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Frechette) too. His remarks are a little lighter, but they provide an adequate footnote. He said:
I have never before listened to a speech so interesting, because it is based on the truth, and when I think of this goodwill meeting it is very encouraging to me. It is you, the electors, who should say what you wish. It is you who pay. We have no status but to serve you and to carry out your legitimate wishes.
One of the rumours we have heard around here-as a matter of fact it was, perhaps part of a public announcement-with reference to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, is that he was leaving this chamber in order to assume duties in another place, possibly in the market place of Montreal. I have also heard a rumour going around today-I hope it is not true, because if it were it would fill me with great sadness-to the effect that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin)

is contemplating leaving this house to enter a different field of endeavour. It seems to me that would be a very tragic blow to this house. I think the former member for Winnipeg North Centre, the former member for Coast Capilano, and the present member for Essex East are the three people to whom I have looked up most consistently in terms both of their deft skill and of a certain liveliness which they injected into the debates of this house, and the thought of the loss of the third of that trio leaves me with a certain sadness.
One of the things about the speech of the Leader of the Opposition which intrigued me was the little lesson in economics which he failed to give to the government and to the Prime Minister. On the whole he attempted to make what he thought was constructive criticism, but he hesitated to suggest any way out of the twin dilemmas which face the government at the present time. I followed what he said. I had read the article in the Reporter magazine to which he referred, and I noticed that whoever had looked over the article in question had lifted out exactly what would fit in with what the Liberals had been talking about a year ago. I wondered why the Leader of the Opposition had not put this into the record from the same article in the Reporter which, incidentally, was written by Arthur Burns, a very orthodox economist who was lately adviser to the President of the United States. The quotation I have in mind reads:
An inflationary psychology is definitely spreading, and it poses a serious threat to our nation's economic health and progress.
It is precisely for this reason that we must seek solutions both promptly and in a constructive spirit. The suggestion, which keeps recurring, that the way to control inflation is to be less zealous about checking recessions is a counsel of despair. If we ever attempt to follow it, we would only add to our troubles, both domestically and internationally.
In other words, Dr. Burns is orthodox.
Our real need is not to weaken anti-recession policies but to improve them so that they will be less likely to release inflationary forces. I must add. however, that improvements in our business-cycle policies will not of themselves suffice to curb the inflationary trend. The problem of inflation which we face is of a long-range character, and a comprehensive policy and some major reforms are required to bring inflation under reasonable control.
Now I think all hon. members probably noticed the rather querulous note which crepi into the Prime Minister's voice when he was answering the Leader of the Opposition as reported on page 62 of Hansard. Describing the problem of inflation and speculating on the answer to it, he said:
There is one of the major problems that economists have not been able to answer today, the

unusual position with which we are faced. I think it requires action on the part of all of us.
I have the unusual feeling, recalling these words, that the Prime Minister was waiting for an economist to come up with the answer. And here is an economist with an answer as far as the United States economy is concerned, though I think it could be translated into Canadian terms. Dr. Burns goes on:
It will take many minds and much effort to work out the particulars of this policy. The way to start, in my judgment, is to amend the employment act so that reasonable stability of the consumer price level will be explicitly included among the high objectives which it is the continuing policy and responsibility of the federal government to promote. Such a declaration of moral purpose by the congress with regard to the price level is the most effective action that can now be taken to arrest the dangerously spreading belief that we are living in an age of inflation. Once that is accomplished, we must go to work not merely on the monetary front, or the fiscal front, or the agricultural front, but on all these and others, without, however, interfering with the essentials of economic freedom.
We need to review the patchwork of special legislation that our government has evolved through the years in the form of price supports, import duties, import quotas, wage regulations, stockpiles, and subsidies-all of which tend to raise prices. We need to devise better defenses against monopoly power, whether it crops up in business dealings or in labour relations. We need to establish local productivity councils, composed of civil leaders, business executives, and trade-union officials, to spot industrial wastes and promote improvements in efficiency. We need to review our tax laws, with a view to carrying out reforms that may spur the nation's productivity. We need to keep a firmer rein on public expenditures in times of advancing prosperity and develop better budgetary controls over the progress of expenditures.
Then Dr. Burns goes on to further suggestions. Now I submit that involved in all these suggestions is a concept and an idea of social and economic planning that everybody seems to do a buck and wing about in the Conservative party whenever they are mentioned. What is the alternative? Many of us remember the speech made by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) the other day when he stood up and extolled the virtues of free enterprise, giving us all the impression that he came from a constituency of independent, rugged individualists who delighted in making out on their own without interference from any quarter. It was a fine speech on the free enterprise ethic, yet what did he say immediately afterwards? He began to talk about government subsidies for the shipbuilding industry to help things out in his part of the country. I do not blame him for asking for these subsidies, but why try to have it both ways? Obviously his constituency is in as much need of subsidies as any other, and in these circumstances, with
The Address-Mr. Fisher these paradoxes to boggle at the words, social and economic planning seems to me completely silly.
Now here is a Canadian economist-at least he is Canadian in origin-to whose work I have referred before, and I wish the Prime Minister would invite him to Ottawa so that he might assist in the solution of some of these problems. I refer to Professor Galbraith who wrote the best seller "The Affluent Society". Professor Galbraith has quite a number of suggestions to make regarding the way out of this dual problem of inflation and unemployment. One of them could really have been considered a year ago, and that is the question of so adjusting our unemployment benefits that if you have a very large amount of unemployment the benefits would go up, and if you had only a small amount of unemployment the scale would go down; in other words, the scale would change with a definite idea of pumping money into the system when it was actually needed.
One of the points which Professor Galbraith makes that we never seem to get clear, despite all the concern we have about production and the gross national product, is that Russia has a much lower gross national product than the United States and yet is able to achieve things on such a scale that they frighten us, all by means of more efficient direction. None of us wants to see here the type of system that the Russians have; I am sure that I am no more and no less of a gradualist with regard to movement in economic terms than anyone else in this house, but we have to face the implications of what is happening elsewhere. One of the paragraphs in Galbraith's book which particularly interested me was this:
Our economy, and the economic theory that explains and rationalizes its behavior, immobilizes all but a minor fraction of the product in private and, from the standpoint of national security, irrelevant production.
In other words, he means such things as lipsticks, breweries, alcohol and similar articles which are by no means part of a nation's vital production. These are quite irrelevant, certainly much more irrelevant than such things as schools, highways and roads. Professor Galbraith goes on:
We have not seen that the problem is far more than one of a bigger budget-that it is one of our attitude toward the goals of the society itself. A society which sets as its highest goal the production of private consumer goods will continue to reflect such attitudes in all its public decisions. It will entrust public decisions to men who regard any other goal as incredible-or radical. We have yet to see that not the total of resources but their studied and rational use is the key to achievement.
One of the most interesting pastimes in which one can engage at this time is going through the speeches of the backbenchers, if
446	HOUSE OF
The Address

Mr. Fisher you do not mind the use ot that term, Mr. Speaker. Almost every one of them has stood up and laid on the line what he would like for his constituency and almost every request has been in the field of public expenditure or of public capital. I think it is time we faced up to the anachronism in our thinking and realized that there is now very little real difference between the question of free enterprise and social and economic planning. We may be able to operate with one and retain the basis of the other but we will have to move on against the whole crisis and have regard to the international situation.
One of the difficulties one encounters in speaking on a topic like this is that one perhaps tends to fulminate more than one should if one is to keep one's arguments reasonable. From my meagre knowledge of economics I believe that the Keynesian system of economics is over the hill. Under that system it was felt that somehow by monetary and fiscal finagling of the entire financial structure of the country you could keep going on or adjust to an even keel. The Prime Minister says the economists do not have an answer. I believe we should conduct a continuing study of the whole field of social and economic planning, placing it on a rational basis instead of having it a piecemeal, ad hoc affair that makes no pattern.
One reason I get excited in this respect is that unemployment in my region is very bad and at this moment approximately 25 per cent of the labour force is unemployed.
Last year I made a certain statement in this house and when I did various hon. members went running around the chamber saying that they would report it back and checkmate the C.C.F. out west. I am going to make that statement again today because it is as true now as it was then. In terms of the financial fibre of this country there is no industry more important than the pulp and paper industry, without excepting the grain business on the prairies. If you want to get a clear picture of it, look at the export trade figures. The pulp and paper industry is in serious trouble. One of the promises extracted from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) last year was that the government in cooperation with the officials of the Department of Finance would study the whole question of fiscal policy in relation to the pulp and paper and forest products industry. There has been unrest and worry in the industry for some time. One thing we do know is that those engaged in the industry in northwestern Ontario have the highest wood costs in the world so far as pulpwood is concerned.
They also have some of the highest transportation costs in the world. Every time


freight rates go up they are in more difficulty and their competitive position is weakened. We know that the southern states have brought more pulpwood forests and mills into production. They have a tremendous advantage over us for their growth cycle is three or four times as fast as ours. On top of that chemical engineers are revolutionizing the process of dealing with low grade species produced in the northeastern and the lake states. Most of our pulp and paper is exported to the United States and our competitors there are in an increasingly strong position.
We have also to face the problem of competition from Russia. There are under construction in Russia two pulp and paper mills with a capacity of 1,000 tons a day; genuine giants. What will happen to the industry in Canada if Russia should decide in future to drop a few hundred tons on the world market? The important but relatively little we do export to Europe and the Caribbean will be lost to us. We need to take a close, hard look at the pulp and paper industry in Canada. I know very definitely that representations have been made to the government from the point of view of management and I wanted to go on record stating the position from the point of view of those engaged in the industry in my particular area.
I received just today from a professional forester in my area a copy of a paper he gave about ten days ago in Sudbury to the Ontario professional foresters' association. He has indicated that many people approached him and said he was a brave man to have given this paper. I want to read a few paragraphs from it in the hope that these words will come to the attention of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I believe it points out clearly some of the problems the forest industry faces at this time. The article is entitled "The Professional Forester in Industry" and was written by Mr. K. W. Hearnden. Portions of it are as follows:
Canadians, in government and industry, are still busily engaged in the conversion of the forest, our most important resource, into revenue and profit dollars and an enviable standard of living without a proper awareness of the possible consequence of neglecting the early initiation of forestry measures. The consequence, suggested by the Canadian Institute of Forestry in a submission to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, is that "the country is in danger of impoverishing its most economical sources of wood". In 1957, Dr. H. R. McMillan, an eminent Canadian forester of 50 years professional experience said, "It is doubtful whether Canada, with its present attention to forest management, can sustain today's annual cut in perpetuity, even by going farther north each decade into virgin forest (at greater cost for logs) or by using a higher proportion of inferior species (thus reducing our competitive ability in the foreign markets upon which we depend)."

I might say that Dr. MacMillan is one of the few foresters I know in this industry who has become a multi-millionaire. I know that as far as our foreign markets are concerned exports are down and a couple of machines in lakehead mills are being closed down and we do not know when they are going to operate again. The following statement is very clear:
Canada does not have an official forest management policy which will ensure the perpetuation of our forest resource and the maintenance of our future world competitive position in forest products. This deficiency is apparent in the legislation of most provinces, whereunder regulations are made to ensure the orderly liquidation of virgin stands and to provide for the levying of stumpage assessments, taxes, rentals and penalties. it can be said, then, that the forester in industry derives little or no support from either the general attitude of the public toward the forest or from existing forest legislation. With but few exceptions, it can be said that he has neither the authority, nor the responsibility for the management of the forest areas with which he is directly concerned.
Later on in the article the writer states:
In adequate forest legislation and public indifference and ignorance have already been suggested a.s deterrents to forest management and to the discharge of professional duties in industry. In addition. several other factors should be mentioned:
1.	Costs-Steady increases in the cost of producing timber during the past ten years are largely attributable to the demands of labour. These increases have had the effect of reducing any margin which might have been made available for forestry.
2.	Forest Management Standards and Objectives- At present the industry has no long term objective in forest management other than the continuous production of essential raw material and the maintenance of a rough status quo in respect of the regeneration of logged sites. Under present conditions, industry is prepared to accept whatever stand conditions may fortuitously develop after logging and assumes that chemistry will solve future problems created by low grade, second growth stands and proliferating silvicultural "slum" areas.
Without silvicultural standards, arbitrary or otherwise, governing regeneration establishment periods, stocking and species requirements, the industrial forester cannot properly manage the forest. This is probably the most contentious single issue amongst foresters and one which must be resolved soon by the profession as a whole.
3.	Authority-With but few exceptions, foresters in industry do not have the authority to manage the forest in any real sense. It is probable that this authority can only be created by enlightened legislation.
That is a very large problem and it ties in closely with costs. Not only are labour costs high but we are getting farther from the mills. It will be a longer time before the forests close to the mills come back than is the case in the southern states or in Russia.
I wish to express a real debt of gratitude to two hon. gentlemen from Toronto on the government side of the house who spoke about education. I only hope they are working in caucus to convince more and more
The Address-Mr. Fisher of their members that action by this government in the field of education would probably be the most popular measure that could be placed on the statute books at this time. I admire the report to which they gave publicity and the arguments they advanced. Certainly the report and their presentation of the situation were not complete but there has been no finer treatment of the subject in this house in the short time I have been here. As a teacher and librarian I expected to find a concern for education among members of parliament when I same to Ottawa but I soon learned that most hon. gentlemen were not interested in the subject in any real, heartfelt way. Therefore I want to heartily congratulate the two hon. gentlemen for having spoken on this topic. They deserve it for standing up and outlining the position of Canadian education vis-a-vis the Russian and for detailing reasons why, when, and where we should move with respect to this field.
While the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) is in the house I want to make a few remarks about Conservatism which might be a nice note on which to conclude because as a life-long Conservative I know he is interested in this topic. A C.C.F. member of parliament was once approached by one of the best lady workers in his whole constituency organization at a meeting at which he had made a resounding, table-pounding speech on the virtues of socialism. She said, "Do you mean to say we are socialists?" He nodded his head and said, "Yes." She said, "Oh, I never knew." This account in the Winnipeg Tribune of January 20 is very enlightening. It has the heading, "Why Are Tories Tories? They Follow Parents' Politics." I am going to put this article on the record because it is so interesting. It is written by Frank Jones and I think the members from Winnipeg should give him a pat on the back. The article reads:
Why are Conservatives Conservatives? According to members of the South East and St. James Women's Progressive Conservative Association asked this question Monday, it's because their mothers and fathers were Conservatives. From the president down, it seems it's a matter of what the rest of your family are.
"My husband was an ardent Conservative," said retiring president, Mrs. F. M. Bastin in her report to the annual meeting. "And I endeavour to live by the Guide motto-I promise to do my best."
Asked why she was a Conservative, a new member, Mrs. I. E. Hansen said she thought the Liberals might be for union with the U.S.A. "But the Conservatives tend to cling to British ties."
Diefenbaker?-"A man of great ability."
What about a television commentator's claim that the Prime Minister has an inflated ego? "Well it would be foolish for a man of his ability to pretend humility."
448	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fisher
Mrs. J. Jenkins, one of Winnipeg's longest standing Conservatives knows why she is a Conservative. "They are loyal to the good old Union Jack and are for the betterment of mankind." She also knows why she does not belong to another party.
This is very interesting.
"Liberals are not for the underdog; the C.C.F. are a bunch of communists and are anti-Christ. Communists represent the devil."
We are getting right to the heart of the Conservative creed here.
Miss H. J. MacNeil, who has worked for the Conservatives in elections for forty years, said, "By far the best party. Sir John A. Macdonald was quite right in his principles. We should pray for the fall of these dreadful communists," she added as an afterthought.
Like nearly every other member asked, new president, Miss Ethel Johnson, said she was first a Conservative because her father was. "I think they are not so much for change as the Liberals. As their name suggests, they are conservative."
How did she account for the word "Progressive" in the title? "Yes, that has puzzled me too sometimes, but I expect there's a reason for it."
Another member, refusing to give her name, said she was quite certain she did not believe in the C.C.F. "I don't know much about them but I know I don't believe in them."
This took me, Mr. Speaker, to an article that I enjoyed very much last year. It deals with another viewpoint of the differences between Conservatives and Liberals. I showed it to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Chambers) and after reading it he just mumbled-I think that is a fair statement-that he figured he was a liberal. Anyway, this gentleman, Mr. Herbert Mc-Closky, did a social science research project analysing in depth what "conservative" and "liberal"-not with capital letters-mean. This article is the result of the long study he made and I know that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) will be interested. It reads as follows:
One of the clearest findings in both studies is that, contrary to claim, conservatism is not the preferred doctrine of the intellectual elite or of the more intelligent segments of the population, but the reverse. By every measure available to us, conservative beliefs are found most frequently among the uninformed, the poorly educated and, so far as we can determine, the less intelligent. There is a sharp decline in the level of information and intellectual grasp as one moves from the more liberal to the more conservative sections of the population . . . The data show clearly, nevertheless, that the most articulate and informed classes in our society are preponderantly liberal in their outlook.
He goes on to say:
Conservatism, in our society at least, appears to be far more characteristic of social isolates, of people who think poorly of themselves, who suffer personal disgruntlement and frustration, who are submissive, timid and wanting in confidence, who lack a clear sense of direction and purpose, who are uncertain of their values and who are generally


bewildered by the alarming task of having to thread their way through a society which seems to them too complex to fathom.
There is another quotation in this regard that I appreciated very much. It is taken from "The True Believer" by Eric Hoffer, published in 1951, and reads as follows:
Far from being the elite or the masters or the prime movers, conservatives tend on the whole to come from the backward and frightened elements of the population, including the classes that are socially and psychologically depressed.
This whole question raises this issue, Mr. Speaker: Are these Conservatives more progressive than conservative? After reading this indictment of the conservative mind I hope that for their sakes they are more progressive than they are conservative. I can only suggest that maybe it might not be a bad idea if the Prime Minister, who has often been said to be a progressive, would drop the "Conservative" from the name of the party so that it would become known as the progressive party. I am sure we would see them in a little rosier hue.
When I make the suggestion I am drawn back to this very interesting article in the Winnipeg Tribune and, comparing it with the conclusion reached in this socio-scientific study, we are left with a real dilemma, something like the dilemma that members of the opposition have been left in when considering the program before us this session.
I am informed that I have a few more minutes. I had intended to speak longer on this particular theme but I see so much recognition on faces in other parts of the house of the pithiness of the words I have quoted that I do not think there is any need to continue. One matter I should like to touch on relates to the Canadian National Railways and the effect of central traffic control and dieselization on the future of divisional points. I have four Canadian National and three Canadian Pacific divisional points in my constituency and there is tremendous concern among the railroaders about pending changes. I have here a letter I received from the council of the town of Hornepayne in northwestern Ontario and it will give some idea why I feel we have to check, watch and demand much more from Mr. Donald Gordon than we have in the past. Last year Mr. Gordon appeared before a parliamentary committee. I do not want to put improper opinions in his mouth but I took from his remarks that he felt there was not much use in going out and telling these people what was going to happen. This letter is addressed to me and it is signed by John Redgrift, reeve of Wickstead township, Hornepayne, Ontario, and reads in part as follows:
Owing to the fact that the prosperity of our community is directly affected by the efficient and

profitable operation of the Canadian National Railways we deem it necessary to criticize the present policy of the present management of this company.
It seems to us that the Canadian National Railways is at present under the control of a group of unrealistic economists and through this control the operations are deteriorating to the point where not only are they unprofitable for the future but are also becoming very unsatisfactory in regards to safe operation. Lay-offs are taking place that cannot help but aggravate the above-mentioned conditions and we herein mention some that directly affect the safe and profitable operation of this great railroad owned by the Canadian people.
First of all, our track, main line and yards. Not only have the section forces been reduced, who are responsible for maintaining this track in condition for high speed operation, they have been given additional mileage to maintain, more switches to keep in working order which means that they must travel additional distances to the scene of their repair work and therefore less time to do the necessary repairs to the track and maintenance work on the switches and yards. This means that the track conditions are deteriorating rapidly, necessitating the issuance of slow orders to the operating trains and a curtailment of their speed to the point where schedules cannot be met, let alone make up time in the terminals.
The terminal and repair forces have been reduced to the point that it is impossible to service a train properly in the terminal time allotted to the schedules of our trains. Therefore trains are leaving not properly inspected and serviced with the result that breakdowns and delays occur enroute between terminals with the accompanying danger of derailments that could be very costly and a serious possibility of fatal accidents. Not long ago, in fact during the Christmas rush, a passenger train left Capreol improperly serviced with the result that the steam generating boilers ran short of water, freezing up several coaches on the remainder of the train. The train stopped at an emergency watering point, this service was frozen up owing to lack of attention. The train proceeded to the terminal where there was no thawing facilties due to the laying off of the boiler attendant last spring and the facilities not re-opened last fall. This train then proceeded to the divisional point where it was delayed eight hours thawing out the steam lines in the coaches. These coaches were our best equipment on the "super continental" and were a complete shambles on the completion of the thawing job, and the 407 passengers on the train, all in a hurry to get to their destination for Christmas were, to say the least, very annoyed and disappointed in Mr. Gordon's claim "service bar none". This type of service does not speak well for the future patronage of this railway by the passengers of our "super" that day.
Our rolling stock backlog of defective cars is steadily mounting and each of these cars that are classed as "loads" represents some dissatisfied customers patiently waiting for their shipment of freight to arrive, and on top of this there is a move on foot to reduce further the repair men and repair points for these cars.
The letter goes on to state that there is tear in the other communities, and in the other divisional points, that they are going to become ghost towns. The value of their property has tumbled. There is a deep dispirited feeling abroad in these communities, and people are moving out. This whole situation involves the question, what is the responsibility of a large corporation when it is the 66968-9-29
The Address-Mr. Clancy bellwether of the community's economy? Does the corporation, and in this particular case the people of Canada, accept certain responsibilities for these bad conditions in these divisional points? This is one of the reasons why I think this government needs to do more planning and more studying on this sort of thing. We now have a terrible situation in these particular divisional points. I shall close on this particular note hoping that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) will get together with the president of the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first join with those who have spoken before me in welcoming and congratulating the four new members who took their seats on January 15. At the same time, I extend my deepest sympathy to the relatives and friends of the late hon. members for Trinity and Springfield who sat with us during the last session. I do this on a personal note because I formed a very close friendship with these two members.
To the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I offer my sincere congratulations; first, upon their having been so honoured and, second, for the excellence of their presentation. Before I get into my prepared text, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) for his recommendation that we adopt the Chinese commune system. He spent a great deal of time quoting from this and that publication. He advocated controls of this and that and the other thing, and I shall take the trouble to inform the majority of my constituents that they are considered by the hon. member to be ignorant half-wits. I must congratulate the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) for having the intelligentsia of Saskatchewan concentrated in his constituency.
I should like to say a few words about my constituency of Yorkton in the province of Saskatchewan, whose economy is based solely on the successful operation of the primary industry of agriculture. The majority of the people are engaged in the production, processing and marketing of agricultural products. The balance are engaged in providing services of one kind or another to the different communities. Since the people in my constituency are, for the most part, selfemployed, they are an independent and selfreliant group.
The city of Yorkton, which is nearly the geographical centre of the constituency, is our largest centre. Yorkton has been well

The Address-Mr. Clancy served over the years by competent aider-men. It is a well planned, clean and pleasant city, and one of the few in which you will find no slums and no shacktown on the outskirts. Yorkton is the distributing centre for that area of the province. The biennial international film festival, sponsored by the Yorkton film council, now has entries from some of the world's best documentary film companies. The golden sheaf award is becoming a prized international award.
The annual Yorkton fair and the autumn agricultural shows are outstanding because of the quality of the exhibits. They are to be congratulated for their success in national and international competition. The farmers of my constituency are engaged in the basic industry of agriculture. The steps taken by the government to implement a long term national agricultural policy, after years of a government with no policy, a government which drifted from one crisis in agricultural to another, are appreciated and are receiving support from the farmers. The practising farmer knows that only when he has a price set-up which will guarantee that the prices he is to receive will not be allowed to fall below a reasonable minimum, only when he has a system of crop insurance which will protect him from financial disaster when his crops are wiped out by natural hazards, can he plan his production to ensure a steadily rising standard of living. The long term national plan for agriculture introduced by this government is designed to bring about the conditions I have mentioned. The steps already taken to implement this plan are on the records of the house. The speech from the throne indicates that the government is proceeding in an orderly manner in the implementation of its agricultural policy.
The attention of the house has already been drawn to a statement in the current review of agricultural conditions in Canada, January, 1959, but I should like to repeat it for emphasis:
Although both cash income and operating expenses advanced during 1958, the greater increase was in cash income and, therefore, realized net income was higher than in 1957.
The trend of 1957 was, therefore, reversed in 1958. This was gratifying. It means that, in general, farm costs rose more slowly than farm income and this widening of the margin between cost and income has eased the cost-price squeeze. The opposition, probably, does not like this because they went up and down the country preaching depression. One almost had the feeling that they would welcome economic disaster, no matter what the cost to the Canadian people, if it could further their own narrow political ambitions. It

would not be the first time in the past 50 years that they have placed party before country.
This improvement in the position of our farmers resulted from legislation introduced by this government. The current review of agricultural conditions in Canada, January, 1959, states:
Support activities under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, will continue to exert a stabilizing effect on farm prices and income.
I should like to draw attention to some of the members who were sitting in this house when this act was passed and their statements with respect to the value of the stabilization act. We shall do that in a proper place and at the proper time. The stabilization act was only one of the measures passed by this government to aid our agricultural community.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed measure to institute a system of crop insurance in cooperation with such provinces as so desire, is of great importance in the prairie provinces. We know only too well the financial loss of a farmer who has his crops wiped out by hail, frost, flood or other natural causes. The loss of a year's income is not lightly shrugged off.
The efforts of the government to sell more of our grain abroad is meeting with success. This action is bringing more cash to the wheat board and, particularly, to producers of wheat. The problem of deficiency payments was studied by the members from the wheat board area and it was studied from every angle. Several problems arose from their discussions. What benefit would the farmer who fed his grain to livestock derive from the plan? What benefit would the grain farmer who had his crop destroyed by hail, flood, et cetera, in one year or possibly in two succeeding years, derive from the plan of deficiency payments? What benefit would the small farmer who marketed a limited amount of grain derive from the plan?
I come from an area into which I can take you and show you permit books of farmers with 20 acres in wheat. What would such a farmer get out of deficiency payments? It began to become apparent that deficiency payments would be a bonanza for a few, and nothing for a great many. The acreage payment was an effort, and a successful one, to make the distribution of the money available fair to all the farmers in the area.
The cost of production on Canadian farms has been an elusive statistic. There appears to be no organization or government department that can provide such figures. The farm income and expenditures survey, a sample survey in nine provinces designed to

provide reliable estimates of (a) farm business income and expenditure and (b) farm family living expenses was carried out last November and December. The survey will be able to provide a clue to cost of production.
Transportation costs have always been a large factor in the cost of production and the cost of living in my constituency, and the proposal of the government to take steps to alleviate the discriminatory effects of the recent horizontal increase in freight rates is extremely welcome. Efforts are being made to increase the net income of the agricultural community, and one method is to lower costs. As I have said, the cost of transportation, both of the materials we need and of our products going to market, is a vital factor in our economy. The people of my constituency look to the St. Lawrence seaway to provide a means of cheap transportation. They feel that the only direct benefit that the seaway can be to us is to provide a cheaper method of moving goods.
My constituents are aware of the fact that many problems involved in the administration of the seaway and regulations for its use must be solved by agreement with the United States. On the other hand, they do not wish to see any group-either a group of ship owners or a labour union-in a position where they could by unilateral action increase shipping costs without regard to the welfare of the country as a whole. They ask only that there be free competition between the carriers using the waterway. I know that I can assure them that this government will see that their interests are protected.
The opposition have continued to try to justify their dark prediction of 1958. Unemployment is still a serious problem, but in the prairie region the situation has improved. I quote from the "Monthly Summary, Employment Conditions, Prairie Region, December, 1958":
The seasonal increase in the number of persons seeking work during the month continued. However, at the month's end there were approximately
3.000	fewer persons registered for work than at the corresponding period last year and there were about
1.000	more unfilled vacancies on hand.
This is not a spectacular change, but it is in the right direction.
As a veteran, it is with pleasure that I welcome the proposed amendments to the Veterans Rehabilitation Act and the War Service Grants Act and, particularly, changes in the Veteran Land Act which give our veteran farmers certain opportunities enjoyed by their neighbours.
Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the hon. member for 66968-9-29J
The Address-Mr. Boivin Hull (Mr. Caron) to the same publication, namely the monthly report on employment conditions in the prairie region. At page 200 of Hansard he produced some rather phenomenal figures, and indicated that his engineers had told him that the cost of winter work or winter construction was 12 J per cent higher, and that in fact it was not worth doing at all, it was so high. But using this publication I should just like to quote to him the comment. It is headed "Winter Employment Campaign, 1958-59", and it reads as follows:
Winter Cost Myth Blasted
The Regina school board received proof in December, that reports on excessive winter construction costs were unfounded.
The board, in considering a quarter million dollar extension to two schools, mindful of possibilities to provide winter work, asked contractors to submit separate bids for winter and summer work.
"The small difference in cost is surprising", commented the board's public relations director. Earlier the board believed the additional expense for winter work would amount to from 10 to IS per cent. However, the three lowest bids quoted winter work only 1.3 to 2.3 per cent higher than summer costs.
I would not suggest to the hon. member for Hull that he send his engineers there but I would suggest that he might pay a visit to Regina and find out how to get cost figures.

Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks, I should like to call your attention to the fact that we are celebrating, this year, the centenary of my native city which, from the point of view of population and industry, is the greatest centre of the constituency I have the honour to represent in this house.	In fact, last
Saturday, January 17, my fellow-citizens of Granby have marked at the city hall the official opening of these festivities, commemorating a century of progress.
On studying history, we note that as far back as 1825, a community had gathered in a certain territory of the township of Granby, as the result of the setting up of a fur trading post by Mr. Richard Frost. Mr. Frost settled on a concession bought from an agent of the governor, and which had belonged to Mr. Hugh McQuarters, one of Colonel Cadwell's associates, to whom the township of Granby had been awarded in 1803. Little by little, that community grew, as the settlers had set up various business establishments and industries. Then, these gentlemen asked that this territory be incorporated into a municipality.

The Address-Mr. Boivin
In 1857,	38 of those village dwellers
signed, in accordance with the law, a petition which was first referred to the council of Shefford, and then to the provincial secretary for submission to the legislative council. The petition was then approved and, on July 1, 1858, a proclamation was issued by the Governor General of Canada, incorporating into a municipality the village of Granby. That proclamation came into force on January 1, 1859 and, on January 17, of the same year, the first elections were held. It is that event that we wanted to celebrate on the same date this year. We wanted to pay tribute to the first mayor of Granby, Mr. Patrick Hachett, as well as to his successors who contributed to the progress of that city in the municipal field, and to our ancestors who preceded us in their respective fields.
During the year, Mr. Speaker, several ceremonies will mark that event. So I should like to offer my most sincere congratulations to those who took this initiative. Their task will be heavy, and I wish them much success. That being said, I invite you, together with my colleagues, to pay us a visit; as soon as you arrive, you will be given the centenary souvenir tie similar to the one I am wearing now. You will receive from the citizens of Granby a cordial welcome, and you may believe me when I say that if you pay a visit to the city called the "princess of the eastern townships" it will be considered as a great honour for each one of our fellow-citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues in extending a cordial welcome and sincere congratulations to the member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman). It is true that the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent had himself introduced his son, but the introduction of this new member is something unique since confederation. In fact, this is the first time that the Prime Minister, accompanied by the father of the newly elected member, introduces that member to the house.
I would also like to extend the warmest welcome to the hon. members for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Fortin) and for Springfield (Mr. Slogan.
I now come to the last member who was introduced. I want to express my congratulations again and extend a warm welcome to my colleague for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) who, after a short absence, has come back to his seat in this chamber.


Before I go on with my speech, Mr. Speaker,
I feel it is my duty to report to the house the decease of the Hon. Jacob Nicol, the former representative of the senatorial division of Bedford, which includes the constituency I have the honour to represent. He had many friends among us, and I am sure that on September 23 last, many were shocked, as I was, to learn that this eminent figure would no more be seen in Ottawa and in the eastern townships. He was born at Roxton Pond, which is located both in my constituency and in the senatorial district that he represented. He first practised in Waterloo, the chief town of the constituency, and later moved to Sherbrooke. He gradually rose to the various levels of public life, serving as a member of the provincial legislature, provincial treasurer, and legislative councillor. He held the post of president of the newspapers Le Soleil, VEvenement, le Nouvelliste de Trois-Rivieres and La Tribune de Sherbrooke; he was vice president of the Banque Canadienne Nationale and of the General Trust of Canada, and a director of several firms. He was appointed to the Senate in 1944. He rendered numerous and important services to many of us, through his advice or otherwise. He disliked publicity but enjoyed giving friendly help. His memory will long live in the minds of many of us. Let us hope that those who gained from his counsel will, in turn, render the same services to others. That is how he would have wanted it. To his wife, his next of kin and his many friends, I offer my most sincere sympathy.
I followed and also closely read the speech from the throne. Reference is made to the visit to be made to this country by Her Gracious Majesty the Queen and His Royal Highness Prince Philip, on the occasion of the official opening of a project that was started, and for the most part carried out, by the Liberal government: the St. Lawrence seaway. We extend to them, as guests of this country, our most cordial welcome.
His Excellency also mentioned the stops made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) in the capitals of the countries he recently visited. I hope that the talks he had on the possibilities of extending trade will lead to something brighter than the prospect of employment for our unemployed in Canada, both during his absence and for the past eighteen months. May I add, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister has given more hope and encouragement to the people of India than to the people of Canada.

It is a fact that all Canadians recognize the necessity of a lasting peace. There is nothing new in this, because the ex-prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, said on many occasions that we had to meet the problem and that the amounts that we were paying to save peace were like an insurance premium for the security of our people. I had the occasion to see for myself that it was worth the trouble when I had the honour to attend, in your company, Mr. Speaker, and in the company of my colleagues of the house, the conference of the parliamentary association of NATO countries, at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris last November. I realized it even more, when we visited our airmen and our soldiers in France and Germany.
The speech from the throne mentions the measures that were taken in view of reducing unemployment by speeding up the national works programs.
We will be asked to approve a bill to assist the municipalities of Canada to undertake public works; I wonder if this aid will really be useful to the municipalities since they will receive grants only for winter works that will cost fabulous sums.
Now, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) for the speech he made yesterday on that subject and also for his suggestions.
I am told that the city of Granby intends to undertake its works only in the first week of April. What will the city be able to do in only three weeks, the closing date of the agreement being April 30? What will the unemployed do in the meantime, and after that date?
The government is said to be pleased at the prospects of an economic upswing.
We depend much on the project I mentioned a few moments ago, which was undertaken by the Liberal government. I read quite recently a report of a press conference given by Hon. George Drew, Canadian High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, on his return to London after a one month visit to Canada. This report was published on January 20 on page 15 of the Montreal newspaper La Presse, and I quote:
No doubt unemployment is now a very serious problem, but the situation cannot fail to improve if we consider the important works to come: works and projects which result for a large part from the St. Lawrence seaway. One can see already (added Mr. Drew), the building of new houses, new apartment blocks, new business establishments, new shopping centres, which will serve the municipalities
The Address-Mr. Boivin along the new seaway, and no doubt the activity will increase in shipbuilding and naval construction; "we have not yet entered our true growing period" said Mr. Drew.
Mr. Speaker, the government should not count exclusively on that project initiated by the Liberals to assure prosperity in the country. I would hope that one day the government will wake up and will adopt legislative measures calculated to promote prosperity, because the project I just mentioned can only help.
It is with pleasure that I heard that we would be asked to make a general study and review of the farm credit legislation, in order to make it more efficient and more useful to the development and the maintenance of a sound and prosperous agriculture. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, as a representative of an agricultural constituency, that proposition pleased me very much. However, I hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness), who is from the west, will realize one day that there is in the east, in Ontario, in Quebec and in the maritimes, a certain number of farmers who deserve to be remembered. I believe particularly that the country should remember that our fellow-citizens were attached to their land long before the buffalo disappeared from western prairies.
The government will ask us to introduce certain amendments in the legislation concerning business practices. We should hope that section 34 of the Combines Investigation Act will be repealed because now a great number of dealers take advantage of that section to offer items at prices so low that they really amount to loss-leader sales being used as a lure to bring in customers and kill or greatly reduce any honest competition.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) stated, like his colleagues, that the financial situation in our country is not, in their opinion, alarming at all, and he paid a tribute to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) when he said, among other things, that he was rather particularly trained for the responsibility which is now his. That reminded me that the minister had the gift of speech rather than that of figures, because, as you will remember, during his last budget speech, he spoke during two hours and ten minutes and said nothing.
After the election campaign conducted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the course of which he promised to cut expenses and lower taxes, it is only logical that we should expect something more than an endurance test. I still remember the Prime Minister stating in the house, when he was in

The Address-Mr. Boivin the opposition, that a promise made by a political leader should be kept. Well, Mr. Speaker, that war-cry calling for a reduction in expenditures and in taxes is not a new one; it is an old one that was uttered by the present Prime Minister as far back as 1946 when he was representing the constituency of Lake Centre. At page 3329, he is reported as saying:
I say that the time has come tor a reduction in expenditures, where they can be made. I do not think anyone would insist that taxes will assure prosperity or increase incomes. When you continue war-time taxation to the extent that taxation is now being continued into the days of peace, it has the effect of harassing business and hamstringing the possibility of providing jobs in Canada at the present time.
It is doing more. It is reducing the standard of living of our people to an extent never before known in this country.
He waited for a long time, but he has now been in power for 18 months. What is he waiting for to carry out what he has been preaching for so long?
As for the Minister of Finance, who also supported the Prime Minister during the two last election campaigns when he was making promises that he could not or would not fulfil, I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the result of his present attitude will be the same as the one he predicted himself once when he stated, as reported on page 95 of Hansard of September 11, 1945:
In the next place, the government has been doing far too much talking about what it intended to do in the realm of housing, leading the people of Canada to expect great things. The fact of the matter is that, unless they have something which they have not yet shown this chamber, they cannot possibly hope to fulfil the promises they made to the people, and many thousands of people, disappointed Canadians, are going to be living under conditions of great hardship this winter because of the failure of the government to make good and fulfil its undertakings to the Canadian people.
If no action is taken immediately, Canadians will be in serious trouble not only this year but also in the next four years, i.e. until the party to which I belong comes back into office at the next election.
The hon. member for Muskoka, Ontario, was an able financial critic of the opposition when he sat on this side of the house, if we judge by the applause from his supporters after his speeches. The member for Muskoka, who now represents Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), hoped to be minister of finance. Because of his age and out of consideration for the services he had rendered and his knowledge, he has been appointed Minister without Portfolio. To resort to his good


offices, I think that the Prime Minister who showed consideration for his past experience when appointing him minister, should re-read an excerpt from one of his addresses to ascertain what he thought of a government such as his government today.
Again, I call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the debates of the House of Commons of October 1945, where I find the following remarks:
I submit that no attempt is made to let the people of Canada and this house know in an intelligible way what their position is.
Is it an unreasonable request? In answering that, I should like to bring to the attention of the house this fact. The other day in England a business man, representing I believe, the chamber of commerce asked the government this question: "Will the government disclose to the country the general outline of its financial proposals for the whole of the next five years?" Hon. members might say that this is going pretty far; nevertheless the chancellor of the exchequer, Doctor Dalton, although I am not sure that it was in answer to this question, said to a public gathering in London recently:
We can follow, through the years immediately ahead, a consistent and developing financial plan.
That is all I am asking. I submit that these figures must be in the possession of the Minister of Finance. It is not conceivable that he has not talked about these things; it is not conceivable that he is not ready to look down the alley. We should know where we are going. Can it be that we are to be kept in a state of tutelage? Is this another instance of what we might call order-in-council government, against which some people in this house have protested? Is there anything in that? Whatever the reason is, I contend that there is no objection to our being given figures at this time. When the war was on, of course, we could not ask for these figures. There was no means of projecting the war expenditures then. I submit, with confidence, that the minister must now be able to calculate, with considerable accuracy, subject to coming back later and saying some of the figures must be altered, how much these war expenditures will come down next year, how much the year after that, and so on. If any businessman came to an annual meeting of his company, showed a deficit of the kind and gave no picture of the future, he would either be sacked on the spot or told to go back and prepare an intelligible picture.
Mr. Speaker, unless the government heeds those remarks of the hon. Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Macdonnell), I am sure that the Canadian taxpayer who, in this case, is the company, will fire the Conservative government as soon as he has a chance to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate our Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) on his speech. I am sure that his remarks displeased many members of this house. He was criticized for having smiled when he made his speech. There has been so much confusion in the government policy, even when the government tried to substantiate it with evidence,

and this goes also for its contradictions, you will admit, Mr. Speaker that many would have smiled at less. He told us about the trip of his predecessor the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent who had already been prime minister for six years. This reminded me that the national anthem "O Canada" had been played in many countries where he visited. The day after his return, on March 17, 1954, he confirmed the fact in his report to the house.
I would admit that I am quite anxious to hear the Prime Minister comment on his recent tour in order to see if he was also welcomed with the national anthem which we are so anxious and eager to see adopted by the house. I would also like to add that it would be a good idea if the ministers who have travelled quite a bit since their party took office should report on their trips to the house. Let us hope that their reports will be brief, otherwise this session will last a long time.
The limited time at my disposal precludes me from discussing the situation of the industry known as the rubber footwear industry. I hope the government will reconsider the fact that this industry needs some protection, if it is to survive.
My colleague, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) has brilliantly described the situation of textile products. I fully support his arguments, even though I am not, as he is, a member of the committee of members from the eastern townships.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has stated that the timid attitude being displayed in regard to our trade relations with the United States is due to the policies followed by the leader of the opposition when he was secretary of state for external affairs. That was obviously not the feeling of the judges who awarded the Nobel prize to Mr. Pearson for the admirable way in which he conducted our diplomatic relations with other nations when he held the office of secretary of state for external affairs. I think it will be a long while before such a tribute is paid to a member of the Conservative government.
As a matter of fact, we could put together the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Secretary of State for External Affairs
The Address-Mr. Boivin (Mr. Smith), and both of them would barely reach the stature of our leader in the international field.
I should like to draw your attention to the fact that a few weeks ago I had the honour to attend the opening of the winter job campaign in Granby; I learned then that there was much to be done in that field, even though the representatives of the government state, in lengthy speeches, that there has been a drop in unemployment.
On December 31, 1958, there were, in the neighbouring municipalities of Granby 834 men and 217 women, that is 851 persons who had applied for benefits to the unemployment insurance office in Granby. There were in that city 1,610 men and 906 women, that is 2,516 persons who had already applied; it means that there was a grand total of 3,367 persons out of work. In 1958 the U.I.C. office in Granby paid out $1,536,342.70 and government supporters would have us believe that the recession is over. Mr. Speaker, the number of applicants, at December 31, 1957, for Granby and vicinity was 3,417, and the Conservatives will say there is a decrease of 104 applications, but 1 will deny that. We have new industries, and there should of course be fewer unemployed; however the number of unemployed has increased; there are all those who could not find a job during the year and are not entitled to additional allowances and, for the same reason, are not registered. That reminds me of the pamphlet entitled: "What Diefenbaker has done to fight unemployment in Canada". Going through it, you will find that it contains blank pages, which shows that he has done nothing. This leaflet, which was distributed during the last election campaign-I got a copy at the time-is of even greater interest today.
Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that we adjourn.

subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN DEBATE ON JANUARY 27

speechtext:
Right Hon. J, G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, arising out of an answer I gave to the Leader of the Opposition as recorded on page 358 of Hansard for January 27, 1959, when he referred to the omission of the mayor of Ottawa and the mayor of Hull from the national capital commission. On that occasion I said, speaking from memory, as follows:
In the Federal District Commission Act provision was specifically made that the mayor of Ottawa and the mayor of Hull should be members of the commission.
I now find that the statement I made was inadvertently incorrect. Under the act as it originally was, section 3, subsection 3, provision was made as follows:
One member shall be appointed by the corporation of the city of Ottawa to hold office during pleasure-
Under subsection 4 of the same section we find this:
One member shall be appointed by the corporation of the city of Hull to hold office during pleasure-
In view of the fact the mayors of the two cities had been members of the federal district commission, I associated that section with the fact they were members and thought it made provision for the mandatory appointment of the mayors, while in point of fact the appointment was made by the council of each of these cities. I thought I ought to point out my inadvertence of yesterday.
